content: Asimina triloba, commonly known as the common pawpaw, is a species of pawpaw native to eastern North America. Its range extends from southern Ontario and New York in the north, westward to eastern Nebraska, and southward to northern Florida and eastern Texas. The common pawpaw is a large shrub or small tree that can grow up to 11 meters in height, with some specimens reaching 14 meters. The trunk diameter typically ranges from 20 to 30 centimeters. Its leaves are deciduous, spirally arranged, and broad-lanceolate in shape, measuring 15 to 30 centimeters in length. The leaves have an acute apex and smooth, entire margins. The flowers of the pawpaw appear in early spring, either simultaneously with or slightly before the emergence of new leaves. Each flower is dark red, measures 2 to 5 centimeters in diameter, and consists of three sepals and six petals. The flowers emit a fetid odor. The fruit of the pawpaw is a large, yellow-green berry that ranges from 5 to 15 centimeters in length. It contains several brown seeds, each 15 to 25 millimeters in diameter, embedded within the soft, edible fruit pulp. On a global scale, the common pawpaw is classified as Very Common (Global GRANK G5). However, it is considered a threatened species in New York and an endangered species in New Jersey. In Canada, it is found only in parts of southern Ontario, where it is classified as Vulnerable (National NRANK N3 and Provincial SRANK S3). The Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources has designated the species as Sensitive, and its populations are actively monitored. The fruit of Asimina triloba is rich in fatty acids, with octanoate being the predominant one. It also contains cis-δ9and cis-δ11-hexadecenoate, as well as cis-δ9-, cis-δ11-, and cis-δ13-octadecenoate. The seeds contain bioactive compounds such as asimitrin, a hydroxylated bis-tetrahydrofuran acetogenin, and 4-hydroxytrilobin, which features a bis-THF ring with hydroxyl groups and an α,β-unsaturated γ-lactone with a hydroxyl group. These compounds exhibit selective cytotoxicity against prostate adenocarcinoma (PC-3) and colon adenocarcinoma (HT-29) cell lines, suggesting potential as chemotherapeutic agents for these cancers. The leaves of the pawpaw contain toxic annonaceous acetogenins, which render them unpalatable to most insects. However, the zebra swallowtail butterfly (Eurytides marcellus) is an exception, as its larvae feed on the leaves. This feeding behavior provides the butterfly with protection from predation throughout its life cycle, as trace amounts of acetogenins remain in its body, making it unpalatable to birds and other predators. The bark of the pawpaw contains additional acetogenins, including asimin, asiminacin, and asiminecin. These compounds are potent inhibitors of mitochondrial NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, making Asimina triloba a promising source of both pesticide and anti-tumor compounds.
